# Architecture

Nuxt Native's goal is React Native/Flutter for the Nuxt ecosystem: Vue
components rendered as real native views, not a WebView. This document is
the honest map of what that requires, what's implemented, and what isn't —
so contributors know exactly where the frontier is.

## Why NativeScript, not a from-scratch renderer

A "true native renderer" needs two things a WebView-based tool (Capacitor,
Ionic) doesn't: a JS runtime with native marshalling (so JS can call
`UIView`/`android.view.View` APIs directly, no bridge-over-HTTP, no WebView
process), and a Vue renderer that creates native view instances instead of
DOM nodes. Building both from scratch is most of what NativeScript itself
is — a mature, years-old project. Reinventing it would be a multi-year
detour before a single native view ever appeared on screen. Nuxt Native
builds *on* NativeScript's runtime and on `nativescript-vue`'s renderer,
and focuses its own effort on the part that's actually missing: Nuxt's
developer experience layered on top of that renderer.

## Why not Nuxt's own build pipeline (Vite/Nitro)

Nuxt's builder assumes a browser target: it generates a client entry that
mounts Vue to a DOM node, and Nitro exists to produce a server response to
hydrate. Neither applies here — there's no DOM node, and `ssr: false` on
native builds means there's no server response either. Rather than fight
Nuxt's builder internals to make it emit something it wasn't designed to
emit, Nuxt Native uses Nuxt only for what it's actually good at in this
context — file-based page discovery, the module/auto-import system, config
— and hands the actual on-device bundle to NativeScript's own webpack-based
toolchain, which already knows how to produce a native bundle correctly.

```
app/pages/*.vue  ──(pages:extend hook)──►  route manifest  ──►  useNativeRouter()
                 ──(nuxt-native CLI scan)──►  .nuxt-native/app.js  ──►  ns run/build
```

Two independent consumers read the same page tree: the Nuxt module (via
`pages:extend`, for editor/type-checking DX and the manifest `vue-tsc` sees)
and the CLI (via a standalone filesystem scan, since `init`/`dev`/`build`
run outside Nuxt's dev server). See `src/build/generate-routes.ts` and
`cli/lib/scan-pages.mjs` — they implement the same file-based routing
conventions independently on purpose, rather than sharing a runtime
dependency between a Nuxt-hooked build step and a standalone CLI process.

| Nuxt module (`src/module.ts`) | Implemented, verified | Registers composables/components auto-import dirs, disables SSR, generates the route manifest template via a real `@nuxt/kit` `pages:extend` hook. Confirmed against a real `nuxi dev` run on Nuxt 4 + `vue-tsc` — the manifest is actually written to `.nuxt/nuxt-native/route-manifest.mjs` with correct route names. (An earlier draft called `addTemplate` *inside* the `pages:extend` callback, which silently produced nothing — Nuxt snapshots its template list before that hook fires. Fixed by registering the template once at `setup()` and only capturing the page tree in the hook.) |
| Route generation (`src/build/generate-routes.ts`, `cli/lib/scan-pages.mjs`) | Implemented, verified | Supports Nuxt's common file-based routing subset: `index.vue`, nested folders, `[param].vue`, `[...catchAll].vue`. Both generators independently produce the identical route name/params for the same page (checked against Nuxt 4's actual `:id()`-style dynamic-segment syntax). Route groups / more exotic Nuxt routing features aren't ported yet. |
| `useNativeRouter()` | Implemented, typechecked | Wraps nativescript-vue's real exports `$navigateTo`/`$navigateBack` (an earlier draft used `navigateTo`/`navigateBack`, which don't exist on that package — caught by `vue-tsc` against the actual installed types). Keeps its own route-name stack since NativeScript's `Page` has no built-in concept of a Nuxt route name. `navigate()` confirmed callable on-device (see below); actual page-to-page transition not separately confirmed yet. |

| Composables (`useGeolocation`, `useCamera`) | Implemented, typechecked, untested on-device | Wrap the optional `@nativescript/geolocation` / `@nativescript/camera` plugins via dynamic `import()`. Fixed: content is now wrapped in `<ScrollView orientation="vertical">` by default, with a `scrollable` prop (default `true`) to opt out for screens like a map or webview where scrolling the container would interfere. Re-verified via a real webpack compile after the change. |

| Tailwind support (`<NFlex>`, `tailwind.config.cjs`/`postcss.config.cjs` scaffolding) | Implemented, verified via a real PostCSS/Tailwind + NativeScript-parser pipeline run; Android-scoped by design, iOS deferred | NativeScript's CSS engine only recognizes a fixed property list — confirmed by grepping every `cssName:` registration across `@nativescript/core/ui/` (not just one file; text-align/letter-spacing/etc. live in separate modules from margin/padding/color). It has no concept of `display`, `position`, `overflow`, or CSS grid at all (layout is chosen by container type — `StackLayout`/`FlexboxLayout`/`GridLayout`/`AbsoluteLayout` — never by a CSS property), and its `transform` value parser (`convertToTransform` in `style-properties.js`) expects literal numbers, not the `var(--tw-translate-x)`-style CSS custom properties Tailwind v3 composes its transform utilities from — so running Tailwind's full generated stylesheet as-is would silently no-op most of it. Fixed scope instead: `tailwind.config.cjs` ships with `corePlugins` as an *allowlist* (not the full utility set) of only the utilities that map to confirmed-supported properties (spacing, color, typography, borders/radius, opacity, shadow, visibility, z-index, and the flex-* properties scoped to `<FlexboxLayout>`) — pinned to Tailwind **v3** deliberately, since v4 dropped the JS-config `corePlugins` API this relies on. A new `<NFlex>` component (a bare, unstyled `<FlexboxLayout>` wrapper) is what flex utility classes (`flex-col`, `items-center`, `gap-4`, ...) actually apply to, the same way flex utilities only do anything on a real flex container on web — verified this is a real, working NativeScript CSS property (not just a name match) by reading `flexbox-layout-common.js`'s property registrations directly. `@nativescript/webpack` already runs every `.css` file through `postcss-loader` and merges in a project's own `postcss.config.js` (confirmed by reading `postcss-loader`'s own `getPostcssOptions` merge logic, not assumed from its config comment) — so wiring Tailwind in needed no changes to the webpack config generation at all, just a `postcss.config.cjs` exporting `require('tailwindcss')`, plus `generateEntry()` now copying a project's own `app/app.css` into `.nuxt-native/app.css` (the exact relative path `app-css-loader` resolves, confirmed by reading its source) on every regenerate. **Verified end-to-end without a device**: ran the real `tailwindcss`+`postcss` pipeline against the actual generated `tailwind.config.cjs`/`postcss.config.cjs`/`app.css`/starter pages in a scratch project, then fed the expanded output through the exact same `css` parser package `css2json-loader` uses — confirmed 11 rules parsed cleanly with plain literal values (`padding: 1.25rem`, `background-color: #4f46e5`, `flex-direction: column`), not CSS variables, meaning NativeScript's property converters will actually apply them. **Scoped to Android for now, by design, not oversight**: `<FlexboxLayout>` on Android delegates straight to a native Java widget (`org.nativescript.widgets.FlexboxLayout`) — no concern there — but on iOS there's no native flexbox engine in UIKit, so NativeScript ports the actual flexbox algorithm to JS and runs it in `onMeasure`/`onLayout` (1,291 lines of JS-side layout math per `FlexboxLayout` instance, vs. `StackLayout`'s 157-line thin native pass on the same platform) — mature and shipped in core, but a real, unmeasured performance question for deeply nested trees specifically on iOS, which already carries the same "unverified" flag as the rest of this framework. Not yet run against a real device (same limitation as everything else needing an SDK/Xcode this sandbox doesn't have). **Two real gaps found from actual retrofits, now fixed**: this initially only merged to a feature branch, so installing the default `github:vastx-tech/nuxt-native` spec got none of it — merged to `main`. And the three config files were only ever written by `create`'s one-time scaffold, so re-running `nuxt-native init` on a project that predated this (the exact way `init` is supposed to bring a project up to date) silently did nothing — `ensureTailwindSetup()` (`cli/lib/tailwind-setup.mjs`) now writes all three from `init` too, only if missing, so it can't clobber a project's own customizations. That first fix then surfaced a second: `init` never installs `tailwindcss`/`postcss` themselves (only `create`'s generated `package.json` declares them, and only `create` runs `npm install`) — `postcss.config.cjs`'s `require('tailwindcss')` threw `Cannot find module 'tailwindcss'` on a real retrofit. Fixed by having `ensureTailwindSetup()` check resolvability (`createRequire(...).resolve()`) and `npm install --save-dev` both packages only when actually missing. Verified all three fixes for real: a scratch project with no Tailwind files gets all three generated; a customized `tailwind.config.cjs` survives a second run untouched; and a project missing `tailwindcss` gets it installed live (confirmed via a real `npm install`), with a second run correctly staying silent once it's resolvable. |
| `useWebSocket()` (`src/runtime/composables/useWebSocket.android.ts`/`.ios.ts`, `cli/lib/websocket-setup.mjs`) | **Android: fully verified on real hardware** — real Gradle build, real install, real device, real remote WebSocket server, open/receive/send/echo all confirmed live. iOS unverified like every other iOS path here. | NativeScript has no global `WebSocket` (confirmed on real hardware: `typeof WebSocket` is `"undefined"`) and no maintained NativeScript WebSocket plugin exists on npm (checked directly, nothing real found). `@nativescript/core`'s own HTTP module uses its own native widget (`org.nativescript.widgets.Async.Http.MakeRequest`, confirmed by reading its Android implementation directly), not OkHttp, so OkHttp isn't guaranteed on the classpath just from depending on core — `nuxt-native init` now adds it as a real Gradle dependency via `App_Resources/Android/app.gradle` (the same real `apply from:` mechanism used for version management, reusing the same `ensureMarkedBlock()` helper — factored out of `app-version.mjs` once this became the second real caller needing "coexist with a project's own content and with another managed block in the same file" idempotency). The Java interop (`okhttp3.WebSocketListener.extend({...})` to subclass an abstract Java class from JS) is confirmed as NativeScript's real, standard convention by reading three independent usages directly in `@nativescript/core`'s own source (`ui/frame/activity.android.js`, `fragment.android.js`, `index.android.js`) before writing this, not invented. Since OkHttp itself has no npm type definitions (a Java library, not a JS one), a minimal ambient `okhttp3.d.ts` was added covering only the classes/methods actually used, keeping the rest of the project's typecheck fully clean rather than silently degrading it. <br><br>**A real, non-obvious bug caught before shipping**: this is the framework's first platform-split composable (`.android.ts`/`.ios.ts`, the same convention `@nativescript/core` itself uses) exposed through the package's `"./runtime/*"` wildcard export. Importing it with the same `.js` suffix every other composable uses (`useWebSocket.js`) fails — reproduced directly via a real webpack compile — because the package's exports-field wildcard resolves to an exact target file *before* webpack's own platform-extension list (`.android.js`/`.ios.js`/`.js`) ever gets a chance to run, and no bare `useWebSocket.js` exists, only the two platform variants. Dropping the suffix (`'nuxt-native/runtime/composables/useWebSocket'`) lets webpack apply its extension resolution to the wildcard-substituted path correctly — confirmed both the failing and working form with real compiles, not assumed. Documented clearly in the composable's own doc comment and the README, since it's a real, easy-to-hit trap for the first person to add a second platform-split composable. <br><br>**Two more real bugs caught only by finishing the on-device verification, not by compiling**: (1) OkHttp 5.x split a `com.squareup.okhttp3:okhttp-android` artifact out of the main `okhttp` artifact, and that artifact's AAR metadata requires `compileSdk` 37+ — a real `checkDebugAarMetadata` Gradle failure against this project's (NativeScript's own default) `compileSdk` 35. Fixed by pinning to OkHttp **4.12.0** (the last pre-split 4.x major, no such requirement) in `cli/lib/websocket-setup.mjs`, rather than forcing every project to bump `compileSdk` just to satisfy one dependency. (2) Android blocks cleartext (`ws://`, non-TLS) traffic by default for apps targeting API 28+, so a real device immediately failed with "CLEARTEXT communication to 127.0.0.1 not permitted by network security policy" — the same class of problem Flutter/React Native solve with a debug-only network security config. Fixed the same way: `App_Resources/Android/src/debug/res/xml/network_security_config.xml` (cleartext permitted only for `127.0.0.1`/`10.0.2.2`/`localhost`, only in debug builds — release builds get no such exception) plus a matching `App_Resources/Android/src/debug/AndroidManifest.xml` overlay referencing it. Confirmed both fixes with real rebuilds, not assumed. <br><br>**The actual verification, end to end, on real hardware**: `@nativescript/types` was added as a real devDependency (neither Android nor iOS ambient globals — `okhttp3` aside — existed before this) and wired into `tsconfig.json`'s `types` field, confirmed clean by the exact "Cannot find name" errors it fixed. A real webpack compile of a 14-page app (the same real, full-sized app used for the MCP client's verification, plus one temporary test page) succeeded. A real `gradlew.bat assembleDebug` produced a real, installable APK. `adb install` put it on a real, physically connected Android device. A real Node.js WebSocket server (the `ws` package, port 8181) was bridged to the device over USB with `adb reverse tcp:8181 tcp:8181`. On launch: `[wstest] open` fired, then `[wstest] message: hello from real ws server` — the server's own greeting, received live. Tapping a real on-screen button (verified by screenshot, then `adb shell input tap` at the button's actual on-screen coordinates) sent `ping from device`; the server logged `received: ping from device` and echoed it back; the device logged `[wstest] message: echo: ping from device`. Every leg of open/receive/send/receive confirmed live, not assumed. iOS has the same "written against Apple's real documented API, never compiled" status as every other iOS path in this framework. |
| MCP client (`src/runtime/composables/useMcpClient.ts`) | Implemented, verified against a real MCP server; not yet confirmed on an actual device | The mobile-viable subset of MCP's "Streamable HTTP" transport — its non-streaming mode. Determined by real, on-device capability checks this session (not assumption): NativeScript's runtime has `fetch`/`XMLHttpRequest` but no global `WebSocket` and no `EventSource` (confirmed via a real diagnostic page logging `typeof` each, run on physical Android hardware), ruling out MCP's stdio transport (no subprocess spawning on mobile anyway), WebSocket transport, and streaming Streamable HTTP (server-initiated messages need `EventSource`-style SSE parsing). What's left — POST a JSON-RPC message, read an `application/json` response directly instead of a stream — is confirmed spec-compliant by reading the real `@modelcontextprotocol/sdk` client transport's own source: it's exactly the code path that SDK itself falls back to against a non-streaming server, not a simplification invented here. <br><br>**Verified against a real server, not just reasoned about**: stood up a real `StreamableHTTPServerTransport` (`mcp-server/test-http-server.mjs`) and ran the exact request sequence this composable uses with plain `fetch` — `initialize` (captured the real `mcp-session-id` response header), `notifications/initialized`, `tools/list`, `tools/call`, with the session id correctly echoed on every subsequent request. This also caught a real, non-obvious behavior difference: the transport's *stateless* mode (tried first) requires every request to be independently self-contained, which doesn't fit a client that initializes once and calls tools afterward — switched to *stateful* mode (also the realistic mode a real remote MCP server would run in), which worked correctly end to end. Also confirmed this file compiles cleanly through the real native webpack build, alongside a real, full-sized, unrelated app (13 real pages) with zero errors and zero changes needed to any of them. **Not yet confirmed**: running inside an actual compiled NativeScript app on a physical device against a network-reachable MCP server — needs real network topology (device and server on the same LAN) this session didn't have available to set up. |
| Pinia support (`isPiniaInstalled()`/`renderAppEntry()` in `cli/lib/generate-entry.mjs`) | Implemented, verified via a real webpack compile with the actual store code confirmed in the emitted bundle | Prompted directly by a user push-back: "install nuxt modules like pinia" doesn't work generically, because most Nuxt modules deliver their functionality through Nuxt's own Vite/Nitro build hooks — hooks the native build never runs at all, since it's a separate NativeScript webpack pipeline end to end (confirmed earlier: only `@nativescript/webpack`'s base config + `nativescript-vue`'s `chainWebpack` construct it). Pinia is the exception, not a special case: its actual store engine is just Vue reactivity with zero DOM dependency. Checked directly, not assumed — downloaded pinia@4.0.3 and `@vue/devtools-api@8.1.5` via `npm pack` and grepped their real dist output: zero references to `document`/`localStorage`/`navigator`/`window` anywhere except a single `IS_CLIENT = typeof window !== "undefined"` guard that every DOM/devtools code path (`registerPiniaDevtools`, the devtools plugin, a file-`saveAs` helper) is gated behind — and NativeScript's runtime never defines a global `window` (confirmed by grepping `@nativescript/core`), so `IS_CLIENT` is always `false` and none of those branches ever execute. `@vue/devtools-api`'s `setupDevtoolsPlugin` import is static (needs to resolve for webpack even though it's never called), so it's pulled in as a real dependency too. Everything Pinia imports from `vue` (`effectScope`, `getCurrentInstance`, `inject`, `markRaw`, `toRaw`, `toRefs`, ...) resolves through the existing `vue` → `nativescript-vue` alias, since `nativescript-vue` re-exports `* from '@vue/runtime-core'` directly (confirmed against its actual entry file), and its pinned `@vue/runtime-core` version comfortably satisfies Pinia's `vue: ^3.5.11` peer requirement. Wired in as opt-in, not forced: `generateEntry()` checks whether `pinia` is resolvable from the project (`createRequire(...).resolve('pinia')`) and only then emits `import { createPinia } from 'pinia'` + `.use(createPinia())` in the generated `.nuxt-native/app.js` — confirmed both branches produce the expected bootstrap. **Verified end-to-end, not just at the config level**: a real scratch project with `pinia`/`@vue/devtools-api` actually installed, a real `defineStore`-based counter store, and a page calling it from `@tap` — compiled with a real `webpack()` invocation (`webpack 5.111.1 compiled successfully`, zero errors), and the emitted `vendor.js`/`bundle.js` were grepped directly to confirm Pinia's real core code and the store's own `useCounterStore`/`increment` logic are actually present in the output, not just that resolution succeeded. |
| HTML tag names (`src/runtime/html-elements.ts`, `src/runtime/vue-compat.ts`) | Implemented, verified with a real webpack compile and the emitted bundle inspected directly | A direct follow-up to a user push-back on "can we compile HTML to NativeScript" — full arbitrary HTML/CSS fidelity is out of scope (that's browser-engine-scale work, not a framework feature; see the README's "HTML tag names" section for the case made against attempting it). What's real and buildable: `nativescript-vue` exposes a public `registerElement(name, resolver, meta)` API — the exact mechanism it uses internally for `<StackLayout>`/`<Label>`/etc (confirmed by reading its element registry directly) — so `div`/`p`/`img`/`input`/`h1`–`h6`/`a`/`strong`/`b`/`em`/`i` and several purely-semantic containers (`ul`/`ol`/`li`/`header`/`footer`/`nav`/`main`/`section`/`article`/`aside`/`form`) now register as real native views this same way. `button`/`label`/`span` needed no registration at all: tag matching is case/hyphen-insensitive (`normalizeElementName`), and nativescript-vue's own `Button`/`Label`/`Span` registrations already collide with those lowercase HTML names. Confirmed this isn't short-circuited by Vue's compiler treating real HTML tag names as literal DOM elements (a real risk unique to these tags, unlike custom names like "StackLayout"): nativescript-vue never uses `@vue/runtime-dom` at all, and its own `NSVElement` constructor calls the same registry's `getViewClass(tagName)` for *every* element vnode regardless of which compiled form produced it — verified by reading `NSVElement`'s constructor and `nodeOps.createElement()` directly. <br><br>One real, compiler-level difference *did* surface, and it took real debugging to pin down: `@vue/compiler-dom` compiles `v-model` on tags it recognizes as native HTML form elements (`input`/`select`/`textarea`) to `withDirectives(vnode, [[vModelText, value]])`, importing `vModelText` from `'vue'` — but `nativescript-vue` has no such export (it re-exports `@vue/runtime-core`, not `@vue/runtime-dom`). Reproduced directly: a real compile of `<input v-model="x">` warned `export 'vModelText' was not found in 'vue'`. Fixed with a new `vue-compat.ts` (re-exports everything `nativescript-vue` does, plus a real `vModelText` modeled on `@vue/runtime-dom`'s own implementation but reading/writing `NSVElement`'s `text` property and listening for the real `textChange` event instead of DOM `input`/`change`), aliased in as `'vue'` in the generated `webpack.config.cjs`. Getting the alias to actually win took a second, genuinely non-obvious round of debugging: a same-order `chainWebpack` override looked correct and even proved itself correct via direct instrumentation (`config.resolve.alias.get('vue')` immediately reflected the override) — but the *final* resolved config still had the old value. Root cause, found by reading `@nativescript/webpack`'s `resolveConfig()`/`applyExternalConfigs()` directly rather than assumed: it scans every dependency for its own top-level `nativescript.webpack.js` and auto-registers it, meaning `nativescript-vue`'s alias-setting chain function gets registered *twice* — once by this project's own explicit `require('nativescript-vue/nativescript.webpack')(webpack)` call, and again by that auto-discovery, which runs *inside* `resolveConfig()` itself, strictly after anything the config factory registers directly, regardless of registration order. A same-order override can never win against that; only an explicit higher `chainWebpack(fn, { order: 10 })` does, confirmed by instrumenting the exact chain before and after applying the fix. <br><br>**Fully verified with a real webpack compile**, not just resolved config: a scratch project with a page using every new tag (`div`/`h1`/`h3`/`p`/`strong`/`em`/`img`/`input v-model`/`a`/`ul`/`li`/`button`) compiled with `webpack 5.111.1 compiled successfully` — zero errors, zero warnings (the `vModelText` warning included) — and the emitted `vendor.js`/`bundle.js` were grepped directly to confirm real `registerElement("div", ...)` calls, the `HtmlParagraph`/`HtmlAnchor`/etc. classes, and `vModelText`/`getModelAssigner` are genuinely present in the compiled output, not just that resolution succeeded. Not yet run on an actual device (same limitation as everything else needing an SDK/Xcode this sandbox doesn't have). |
| Gradle memory tuning (`ensureGradleMemorySettings()` in `cli/lib/gradle-tuning.mjs`) | Implemented, verified with a real clean rebuild | Directly reported: "the Gradle building process... taking too much memory." Traced to `@nativescript/android`'s own scaffolded `platforms/android/gradle.properties`: `org.gradle.jvmargs=-Xmx16384M`, a flat 16 GB Gradle daemon heap ceiling baked into the template regardless of the machine actually running the build. Confirmed against the reporting user's real machine: `Get-CimInstance Win32_ComputerSystem`/`Win32_OperatingSystem` showed 5.74 GB of *total* physical RAM — a heap ceiling nearly 3x the entire machine's memory. This plausibly explains more than just slowness: the same session hit repeated, unexplained `'gradlew.bat' is not recognized` spawn failures from the CLI's own child-process invocation (confirmed via `android-plugin-build-service.js`/`gradle-command-service.js`'s source that both just do `spawnFromEvent('gradlew.bat', ...)` relying on `cwd`) despite the file demonstrably existing and running fine when invoked directly — severe memory pressure is a known cause of intermittent Windows `CreateProcess` failures, though this wasn't isolated as the sole cause. <br><br>Confirmed this file has no built-in App_Resources override the way `app.gradle` does (no reference to `gradle.properties` anywhere in the `nativescript` CLI's own source — it's scaffolded once by `@nativescript/android`'s own template copy during `platform add`, never regenerated on subsequent `prepare`/`build` calls), so a one-time patch immediately after `platform add` is durable. `ensureGradleMemorySettings()` computes a replacement `-Xmx` from the machine's actual total RAM (35%, clamped to 768 MB–3 GB — there's no real benefit to a NativeScript app's build ever exceeding ~3 GB of daemon heap even on much bigger machines), adds `kotlin.daemon.jvmargs` (Kotlin's compiler runs its own separate JVM, also worth capping) and `org.gradle.workers.max=2`, and marks the file with a comment so reruns never clobber a value a project has since customized. Verified the computed values are sane across a realistic range (2 GB machine → 768 MB floor; 5.74 GB → 2057 MB; 16 GB+ → 3072 MB ceiling, confirmed by direct calculation, not just eyeballed), confirmed idempotency (byte-identical file on a second run), and — the real test — reran `gradlew.bat --stop` then a full clean `assembleDebug` on the actual affected project with the new ~2 GB ceiling: identical successful build (57 tasks executed, 42 up-to-date) with a fraction of the memory. |

Invoking the resolved config directly (not through the real `ns` CLI, which supplies more `env` context) now produces a complete, valid webpack `entry` config correctly referencing the generated `.nuxt-native/app.js`; only a harmless "Cannot find NativeScript CLI path" warning remains, expected since we're not going through the real CLI. **Fully verified past this point**: running an actual `webpack(config, callback)` compilation (not just resolving the config object) against a fresh scaffold now completes with **zero errors**, emitting real `bundle.js`/`vendor.js`/`runtime.js` — vue-loader, ts-loader, and every native-specific transform (worker-loader, native-class-downlevel/strip-loader) all working together correctly for the first time. | `typescript`/`tsconfig.json` for the native build | Implemented, verified via a real webpack compile | Three compounding bugs, found by running an actual `webpack()` compilation against a fresh scaffold (not just resolving config) after the `main` fix above got far enough to reach real `.vue` compilation: **(1)** `ts-loader` (a dependency of `@nativescript/webpack`) peer-depends on `typescript`, which was never added to generated projects — `@nativescript/webpack` only lists it in *its own* devDependencies (used to build itself, never installed transitively for consumers). Confirmed by reading `ts-loader`'s `compilerSetup.js`: when `require('typescript')` throws, it swallows the error into an unused message and presses on with `compiler` left `undefined`, crashing later on `compiler.sys.fileExists` — exactly the `Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'fileExists')` a real user hit. **(2)** The generated `tsconfig.json` was Nuxt's usual references-only shell pointing at `.nuxt/tsconfig.*.json`, which only exists after `nuxi prepare` runs (never part of this framework's actual workflow) — useless to `ts-loader`, which reads this file directly for real `compilerOptions`. Replaced with a real, standalone config. **(3)** Two further rounds against a real compile: including `nuxt.config.ts` put it in scope for `ForkTsCheckerWebpackPlugin` (which only activates once `typescript` is an actual dependency — fix (1) turned it on), and it fails type-checking there since `defineNuxtConfig` is an ambient global only Nuxt's own generated types provide; excluded it. Then `TS18003: No inputs were found` — TypeScript's `include` glob-matching filters by a hardcoded extension list (`.ts`/`.d.ts`, plus `.js` only with `allowJs`) regardless of what the glob pattern spells, so listing `*.vue` explicitly did nothing and nothing else matched; added `allowJs: true` so the generated `.nuxt-native/app.js` counts as a root file. After all four fixes: `webpack 5.111.1 compiled successfully`, zero errors, on a fresh `create` scaffold. |
| `"type": "module"` in generated `package.json` | Fixed — removed entirely | Same real user, further downstream (the actual `ns run android` device deploy step, past a successful webpack compile): `ReferenceError: require is not defined in ES module scope` inside `platforms/android/build-tools/jsparser/js_parser.js` — a plain CommonJS script *shipped by `@nativescript/android`'s own runtime tooling*, not something this framework generates or controls. Node determines a `.js` file's module type by walking up to the nearest `package.json`; that vendored file has no closer one of its own, so it inherited `"type": "module"` from the project root and got misinterpreted as ESM. Unlike the earlier `webpack.config.cjs` fix, renaming isn't an option here — this file is regenerated by `@nativescript/android` itself on every `ns platform add`. Fixed at the root: removed `"type": "module"` from the generated `package.json` entirely. Verified safe: none of our own generated files need it (`.nuxt-native/app.js`'s `import` syntax is only ever parsed by webpack's own module system, never Node's `require`/`import`; `webpack.config.cjs` is unambiguous regardless of `"type"`) — re-ran the same real `webpack()` compile used to verify the fixes above and it still succeeds with zero errors. |

Directly replicating the CLI's own TS-parsing logic (`ts.transpileModule` + eval, same as `project-config-service.js`) against their file's content extracted `bundlerConfigPath` correctly, ruling out a parsing bug in our generated config. Leading theory: `init`/`dev`/`build` invoke `ns` via `npx --yes nativescript ...`, which resolves from npx's own cache rather than the project's `node_modules` — a stale cached CLI build predating `bundlerConfigPath` support would silently ignore it and fall back to the default, matching the error's exact wording (the fallback branch, not the one used when a custom path is recognized). Fixed pragmatically either way: `nativescript.config.ts` now also sets the older `webpackConfigPath` field to the same path — `bundlerConfigPath` falls back to it internally, so an outdated CLI that only understands the older field still resolves correctly. Neither field was ever set. Read `getEntryPath()`'s and `getProjectRootPath()`'s source directly to confirm `main` resolves relative to the project root (`process.cwd()`), not `appPath`. Fixed by setting `main: '.nuxt-native/app.js'` in both generated files (the constant now lives in `generate-entry.mjs` as `ENTRY_FILE`, imported by both, so the path can't drift out of sync between them). Verified by invoking the generated `webpack.config.cjs` directly on a fresh scaffold: it now resolves to a complete `entry` object correctly listing `.nuxt-native/app.js`, where it previously threw immediately. |
| Components global registration (`<NPage>` etc.) | Fixed | Same real user's device run — this got past `webpack.config.cjs`/`typescript`/`type:module` and past `ns run android`'s full build+install+launch (first time the app has actually run on a physical device), then crashed at Vue's `setup()` with `ReferenceError: useDevice is not defined`. Two separate gaps surfaced by this: components had no registration mechanism at all in the native bundle (Nuxt's `addComponentsDir` only registers globally for Nuxt's *own* build, which the native path never goes through), and composables had no auto-import either (see next row). Fixed the component half: the generated `.nuxt-native/app.js` bootstrap now imports `<NPage>`/`<NActionBar>`/`<NTabs>` from a new `nuxt-native/runtime/*` subpath export and registers them globally via `createApp(...).component(...)`, mirroring what Nuxt's own auto-registration does — the same mechanism (Vue's app-level component registry), just invoked directly. | Auto-imports reaching the on-device bundle (`cli/lib/auto-imports.mjs`, `cli/lib/auto-import-loader.cjs`) | **Fixed, verified end-to-end via a real compiled bundle** | The gap this row used to describe: composables (`useDevice`, `useNativeRouter`, etc.) had no auto-import in the native bundle, only in Nuxt's own separate build (`addImportsDir`). Not fixed with `unplugin-auto-import`/`unimport` (Nuxt's own real mechanism) directly — confirmed `unimport`'s package.json `exports` has no CJS entry at all, and `@nativescript/webpack`'s own bin loads `webpack.config.cjs` with a plain, synchronous `require(configPath)(env)` with no Promise/ESM handling whatsoever (read directly in `@nativescript/webpack/dist/bin/index.js`) — so an ESM-only package can't be consumed from that config file. Built a small first-party loader instead, mirroring unimport's real strategy (a fast identifier scan, skipping names a file already imports or declares itself) rather than a lesser substitute. `generateEntry()` now also writes `.nuxt-native/auto-imports.json` (nuxt-native's own composables, hand-listed same as `RUNTIME_COMPONENTS`, since `useWebSocket`'s platform-split needs its real suffix-less specifier and can't be safely directory-scanned; plus one entry per file in the project's own `app/composables/`), and `ensureWebpackConfig`'s generated config registers the loader as two `enforce: 'pre'` rules. <br><br>**A real, non-obvious bug caught only by inspecting the actual compiled bundle, not by "compiled successfully"**: `ts-loader` runs with `transpileOnly: true` here, so an unresolved bare identifier is not a build error, only a runtime `ReferenceError` — meaning a naive test that just checks the build didn't fail proves nothing. The first version of this loader prepended import lines at the very top of the source string — correct for a plain `.ts` file, but for a `.vue` SFC's split `<script>` sub-request, confirmed by reading `vue-loader`'s own `dist/index.js` directly that it re-parses *the entire raw SFC file* (template and script together, freshly read from disk) for every sub-request, not an isolated script fragment — so those prepended lines landed *before* `<template>`, outside every recognized SFC block, where vue-loader's own block-extraction silently discards them. Confirmed by grepping a real compiled bundle: the composable call sites (`useDevice()`, `useWebSocket(...)`) were present, but the import statements were not, meaning the app would have crashed at runtime with the exact `ReferenceError` this whole fix exists to prevent. Fixed by locating the actual `<script ...>` opening tag and injecting right after it instead of at position 0. <br><br>Also found and worked around: the webpack rule's declarative `resourceQuery: /type=script/` condition (meant to exclude the sibling `<template>` sub-request) doesn't reliably hold in this project's actual, `@nativescript/webpack`-merged config — confirmed via direct loader instrumentation that the function *did* fire for the template sub-request despite the resolved rule object correctly showing that condition. Root cause not fully chased into `@nativescript/webpack`'s own config-merging internals; instead made correctness the loader's own responsibility with an explicit runtime guard (`if (this.resourceQuery && !/type=script/.test(this.resourceQuery)) return source`) rather than depending on the declarative condition alone. <br><br>**Verified past "it compiles"**: a real page using `useDevice()`, the platform-split `useWebSocket()`, and a project-level `app/composables/useGreeting.ts` — all three with zero import statements written by hand — was compiled with a real `webpack()` run, and the emitted bundle was read directly: all three now resolve to correct `__webpack_require__(...)` calls (`useWebSocket` correctly to the `.android.js` variant, confirmed the platform-split case works through auto-import too, not just explicit imports), and the call sites use the properly-bound module exports. Components (a project's own custom `.vue` components, e.g. `HomeScreen.vue`) are a separate mechanism in real Nuxt (component discovery, not `unimport`) and are **not** covered by this fix — still need an explicit relative import. |

| `ForkTsCheckerWebpackPlugin` memory limit (`cli/lib/webpack-config.mjs`) | Implemented, verified with a real crash reproduced and then fixed | Found while verifying the auto-import fix above, not reported separately: `@nativescript/webpack`'s base config registers this plugin (a *separate* Node process just for type-checking) whenever `typescript` is a dependency — true for every nuxt-native project — with a flat `memoryLimit: 4096` (4 GB), independent of the machine actually running the build, the exact same class of problem `ensureGradleMemorySettings` already fixed for Gradle's own heap ceiling. Reproduced directly and repeatedly on the same 5.74 GB machine: `Fatal process out of memory` / `RpcExitError` / `"probably out of memory... check the memoryLimit option"`, tracing to this exact plugin. Confirmed `ts-loader` itself already runs with `transpileOnly: true` in the same base config — meaning this checker adds no build-time benefit the main compile actually depends on, only in-build type-error reporting a project already gets another way (its own `vue-tsc`/`tsc` script, or the editor's TS server) — so disabling it trades nothing away on a small machine. `ensureWebpackConfig`'s generated `webpack.config.cjs` now inspects `os.totalmem()` at build time: below 8 GB, deletes the plugin from the resolved `webpack-chain` config entirely (`config.plugins.delete(...)`, confirmed present first via `config.plugins.has(...)`); at or above 8 GB, tapers its `memoryLimit` proportionally instead of removing it (`config.plugin(...).tap(...)`). Verified on the actual affected machine: confirmed the plugin is present by default, confirmed it's correctly absent from the resolved config after this fix, and confirmed a real webpack compile still succeeds without it. |

Fixed by adding a `webpack.chainWebpack` alias in the generated `webpack.config.cjs` mapping that exact specifier to the project's own CLI-generated `.nuxt-native/route-manifest.mjs` — the same composable source now resolves correctly in both Nuxt's build and the native one, no fork needed. Verified via a real `webpack()` compile against the actual installed package: compiled successfully, and correctly code-split `details/[id].vue` into its own chunk, confirming the manifest's dynamic `import()` resolves too. |

The controls run everything inside a real `vscode.window.createTerminal()`, not a headless spawned process — confirmed by reading NativeScript's own `key-command-helper.js` that `ns run`'s interactive key commands (`r`/`R`/`w`/Ctrl+C) require a real TTY (`stdin.setRawMode`) and silently fall back to an unwired IPC listener otherwise, which a plain `child_process.spawn` with piped stdio would hit. `ns device --json`'s exact output shape was confirmed by reading `ListDevicesCommand`'s source, not guessed. Verified as far as possible without a running VS Code instance: compiles cleanly against the real `@types/vscode` API (`npx tsc`), and packages successfully with `@vscode/vsce` into a structurally valid `.vsix` (`@vscode/vsce@4` itself has an ESM/`parse5` interop bug on this Node version — pinned to `@vscode/vsce@^3.9.2`, which doesn't). **Not verified**: has never actually been loaded into a VS Code extension host and clicked through — that requires a running VS Code instance this environment doesn't have. |
| MCP server (`mcp-server/`) | Implemented, verified end to end with a real MCP client against a real device | Exposes `doctor`/`build`/`lint`/`clean`/`analyze`/`version`/`list_devices`/`install_and_launch`/`read_logs` as MCP tools, each calling the exact same `cli/commands/*.mjs` functions the real CLI uses — no separate implementation to drift out of sync. The one real technical risk: this server talks over **stdio**, meaning stdout *is* the JSON-RPC protocol channel, but `doctor()`/`build()`/etc. `console.log` directly and spawn child processes (`ns info`, `ns build`) that inherit real stdio — either would corrupt the connection. Fixed at the shared layer: `cli/lib/run.mjs` now exports `withCapturedOutput()`, an ambient module-level toggle that makes `run()` pipe+buffer instead of inherit, and captures `console.log`/`console.error`, restored even if the wrapped function throws — with zero changes needed to any of the five existing command files, and zero behavior change for the real CLI's own direct terminal usage (toggle defaults off). Verified directly: ran `doctor()` through it for real and confirmed zero output reached the surrounding process's actual stdout, with the full 13-check report correctly captured instead. **Verified end-to-end, not just at the unit level**: used the MCP SDK's own real `Client` + `StdioClientTransport` (not a mock) to spawn the real server and drive it over the real protocol — `listTools()` returned all 8 tools; `doctor` returned the complete captured report; `list_devices` correctly surfaced a real, pre-existing, legitimate error (`ios-device-lib` `ENOENT` — no iOS tooling on this Windows machine, not a bug here); and with a real connected Android device, `install_and_launch` performed a real `adb install`+`am start` and `read_logs` returned real, current `logcat` output confirming the app actually launched. |

## Roadmap

**Done**, moved out of "future work": a real Android device run completed
successfully (build, install, launch, render) after fixing everything that
run surfaced (`webpack.config.cjs`, `typescript`/`tsconfig.json`,
`"type": "module"`, `main`/`bundlerConfigPath`/`webpackConfigPath`) — see
the status table above for the full trail; and the UI kit now covers
buttons/text/input/card/switch/spinner/avatar/badge/divider/bottom-sheet
/modal, past the original `<NPage>`/`<NActionBar>`/`<NTabs>` set.

1. Wire `unplugin-auto-import`/`unplugin-vue-components` into the
   NativeScript webpack build the CLI hands off to, so composables/
   components auto-import identically in editor DX and on-device (right
   now native pages need explicit imports — see the "Auto-imports reaching
   the on-device bundle" row above).
2. iOS has never been run end to end — everything verified on-device so
   far is Android. `ns platform add ios`/`ns build ios` need an actual
   Xcode install this sandbox doesn't have.
3. Further UI kit components (list, action sheet, tabs-as-navigator rather
   than the current raw `<NTabs>`) and a real device confirmation for the
   ones just added (`<NButton>` etc. are verified via webpack compile only
   so far, same caveat every fresh addition here starts with).
4. Port more of Nuxt's file-based routing conventions (route groups,
   layouts-equivalent) into `generate-routes.ts`/`scan-pages.mjs`.
5. The VS Code extension (`vscode-extension/`) now exists at MVP scope —
   see its status-table row. It has never been loaded into an actual VS
   Code window; that's the next real test for it, the same way a real
   Android device was the real test for everything else here. Also not
   yet done: publishing it to the Marketplace (needs a publisher account
   this repo doesn't have set up), and packaging/publishing it isn't
   wired into any release process yet.
6. CI: a real device-farm or simulator smoke test for iOS, now that
   Android has one manually.
7. Tailwind/`<NFlex>` support landed Android-scoped on purpose (see its
   status-table row) — the two follow-ups once iOS gets real device access:
   an actual on-device (not just pipeline-level) confirmation that
   Tailwind utility classes render correctly, and a real nested-`FlexboxLayout`
   layout-cost benchmark on iOS hardware (using NativeScript's own
   `Trace.categories.Layout` plus Xcode Instruments' Time Profiler) before
   deciding whether `<NFlex>` is safe as iOS's default primitive too, or
   needs a lighter-weight iOS-specific fallback.
8. `<NGrid>` (a real `<GridLayout>` wrapper) doesn't exist yet — Tailwind's
   `grid-cols-*` utilities can't map to it the way flex utilities map to
   `<NFlex>`, since NativeScript's grid is configured via `columns`/`rows`
   template-string properties, not a CSS property at all. Needs its own
   translation layer, not just an allowlist tweak.
9. Publish to npm once iOS gets the same real-device confirmation Android
   has. Until then, install from
   `github:vastx-tech/nuxt-native` (see README) — that install path only
   works at all because `package.json` has a `prepare` script that runs
   `nuxt-module-build build`; `npm install`'s git-dependency flow runs
   `prepare`, not `prepack` (verified by installing the pushed repo into a
   scratch project and checking what actually landed in `node_modules`).
10. `useWebSocket()`'s iOS implementation needs the same on-device
    confirmation every other iOS path here still needs (Android is now
    fully verified on real hardware).
